title: Chest — massive pleural effusion
summary: A white-out, and the one sign that tells you whether it is fluid or collapse.
text:
The patient's right hemithorax is completely opaque. Fluid has a similar radiographic density to soft tissue and is much whiter than air-filled lung, so fluid in the pleural space can obscure the underlying lung.

The decisive sign is what the mediastinum does. Fluid takes up space and pushes it away; collapse loses volume and pulls it towards the abnormal side. Here the trachea and the heart have been shoved to the left, so this is a large effusion, not a collapsed lung.

The adjacent model illustrates the anatomical relationships relevant to a large pleural effusion.
reading: Inspect the opacity for air bronchograms - air-filled bronchi outlined by denser lung. Their presence does not exclude pleural fluid with adjacent compression atelectasis.

Find the mediastinum: trachea, carina, heart borders. Displacement away suggests increased volume or pressure; displacement towards suggests volume loss. A central mediastinum alone does not establish the cause of the opacity.
Look for a meniscus — fluid rides higher at the chest wall than in the middle. In a complete white-out it may be gone.
A decubitus film or, better, ultrasound tells you whether the fluid moves and how much there is, and marks the safe spot to drain.
Then look for a cause: a mass at the hilum, rib destruction, an unusually small hemithorax.

questions.prompt: Why does leftward mediastinal displacement favor a large right pleural effusion over isolated right-lung collapse?
questions.answer: The effusion adds volume and pushes the mediastinum away; isolated collapse loses volume and generally pulls it towards the affected side.
questions.explanation: Use displacement to assess volume gain or loss in the opaque hemithorax. An effusion can also compress the underlying lung.

questions.prompt: In which anatomical space does the fluid in this case collect?
questions.answer: The pleural space, between the visceral and parietal pleura.
questions.explanation: The fluid lies outside the lung and can compress it. The pleural space surrounds the lung rather than forming part of its airways.

title: Chest — right middle lobe pneumonia
summary: The silhouette sign, and how a lost border tells you which lobe is filled.
text:
A hazy opacity in the patient's right mid zone, and – the point of the case – the right heart border has gone. The middle lobe lies directly against the right atrium, so when its alveoli fill with exudate there is no longer air next to that border and the line vanishes. The hemidiaphragm stays sharp, because the lower lobe is still aerated.

That is the silhouette sign, and it localises disease without a lateral film: lose the right heart border and it is the middle lobe; lose the right hemidiaphragm and it is the lower lobe; lose the aortic knuckle or left heart border and it is the lingula or the left upper lobe.
reading: Find the opacity, then ask which border it has erased. That names the lobe.

Look inside it for air bronchograms - black branching airways against denser lung. They show air-filled bronchi surrounded by less aerated parenchyma and can occur in consolidation or compression atelectasis.
Check volume: consolidation fills the lobe without shrinking it, so the fissures stay put. A shifted fissure means collapse.
Confirm on the lateral if there is one: middle lobe disease sits as a wedge in front, pointing at the hilum.
Then look for complications — an effusion, a cavity, a mass behind the pneumonia — and repeat the film in six weeks if the patient is a smoker.

the middle lobe lies against it — no air, no line
the upper limit of the middle lobe, and it has not moved
still sharp — the lower lobe is spared
clear: the upper lobe is not involved
crisp, because the lingula beside it is still aerated

questions.prompt: The right heart border is obscured while the right hemidiaphragm remains distinct. Which lobe does this pattern localize the main opacity to?
questions.explanation: The middle lobe lies beside the right atrium. Increased density there can erase the right heart border, whereas the lower lobe contacts the hemidiaphragm.

questions.prompt: If you find black branching airways within the opacity, what do they represent?
questions.answer: Air bronchograms: air-filled bronchi outlined by denser surrounding lung.
questions.explanation: They can support consolidation, but do not identify the organism. They can also occur in compression atelectasis, so they do not categorically exclude collapse or an accompanying effusion.

title: Chest — pneumothorax on expiration
summary: A line, and nothing beyond it. Plus the trick that makes a small one visible.
text:
An expiratory film. On the inspiratory film taken at the same sitting the pneumothorax is barely there; on expiration, the lung contains less air and appears denser, so its contrast with the pleural air increases and the edge can stand out.

What you are looking for is a thin white visceral pleural line with no lung markings beyond it. Visible lung markings beyond a suspected line favor a skin fold or another mimic; a true visceral pleural line has no lung markings peripheral to it.

The patient has had both breasts removed and a chemotherapy port inserted – worth naming, because hardware and previous surgery are part of reading any film.
reading: Follow the lung edge round: a fine white line parallel to the chest wall, with black and nothing else outside it.
If you are unsure, an expiratory film exaggerates it — as here.

Assess the patient as well as the film: breathlessness can occur without tension. Suspected tension pneumothorax with severe respiratory or haemodynamic compromise is an emergency and treatment should not await further imaging.
Check the apices in a supine film differently: air collects anteriorly and basally instead, giving a deep sulcus sign rather than an apical line.
Then account for every piece of hardware, and look for the cause — a rib fracture, a bulla, a line insertion.

questions.prompt: Which combination of findings identifies the left pneumothorax on this film?
questions.answer: A visceral pleural line with no lung markings peripheral to it.
questions.explanation: The line marks the retracted lung surface. The unmarked region outside it contains pleural air. Lung markings beyond a suspected line instead favor a mimic such as a skin fold.
structures: Air in the left pleural space

questions.prompt: Does the central trachea on this film by itself exclude tension pneumothorax?
questions.answer: No. Tension pneumothorax is a clinical diagnosis.
questions.explanation: Assess respiratory and haemodynamic status. Breathlessness can occur without tension, and tracheal position alone does not establish or exclude tension physiology.

title: Chest — heart failure
summary: Five signs to look for as pulmonary venous pressure rises.
text:
An 83-year-old man with previous bypass surgery, now breathless. The film shows an enlarged heart, dilated upper-lobe vessels, distinct Kerley B lines and a little fluid tracking into the horizontal fissure.

A useful teaching sequence as pulmonary venous pressure rises is: upper-lobe blood diversion first, then interstitial oedema with Kerley B lines and peribronchial cuffing, then alveolar oedema, and pleural effusions throughout. Remembered as ABCDE: Alveolar oedema, Kerley B lines, Cardiomegaly, Dilated upper lobe vessels, Effusions.
reading: Heart size: on a PA film the cardiothoracic ratio should be under 0.5. On an AP or a portable film it is magnified, so a big heart there means less.
Upper-lobe vessels: normally smaller than the lower-lobe ones because of gravity; equal or larger is diversion.

Kerley B lines: short horizontal lines reaching the pleural surface at the bases - thickened interlobular septa, which support interstitial oedema in this clinical setting. Interpret them with the rest of the film and clinical context.
Fissures: fluid thickens them, which is often the earliest effusion you can see.
Then the costophrenic angles, and any alveolar shadowing spreading out from the hila.

labels.note: wider than half the chest on a PA film

questions.prompt: What anatomical structures produce the short peripheral Kerley B lines described in this case?
questions.explanation: Fluid in these septa produces an interstitial oedema pattern. Interpret the lines alongside the enlarged heart, vascular prominence and pleural fluid described here.

questions.prompt: What does the fluid tracking in the horizontal fissure represent anatomically?
questions.answer: Pleural fluid within an interlobar fissure.
questions.explanation: The horizontal fissure is a pleural boundary between the right upper and middle lobes. Fluid can thicken its normally thin outline.

title: CT thorax — the same middle lobe
summary: What the hazy shadow on the plain film actually looks like.
text:
A CT from the same 67-year-old man's right-middle-lobe pneumonia case. On the plain film the middle lobe pneumonia was a vague haze that erased the right heart border; here it is a sharply bounded wedge of lung with air bronchograms running through it, stopping dead at the fissures.

That is the value of CT in the chest: it separates what the radiograph superimposes, and it shows the anatomical boundary — a lobe — that helps localize the consolidation.

Patient's right on your left, anterior at the top. The 3D atlas illustrates related transverse anatomy. It is not registered to this patient's image, so its cut level and the structures intersected may differ.
reading: Lung windows first: consolidation is white lung with black branching bronchi running through it.
Then follow the fissure: consolidation confined to a lobe has a lobar distribution. This localizes the abnormality but does not by itself establish the cause.
Look behind and around it for a mass or an obstructed bronchus, especially in a smoker.
Then soft-tissue windows for effusion, empyema and lymph nodes.
Finally compare with the plain film and see which sign on the film each CT finding produced.

labels.note: anterior and to the patient's right, up against the heart
still open and full of air — an air bronchogram
the border the consolidation rubs out on the plain film

questions.prompt: Which lobe is consolidated here and accounts for loss of the right heart border on the paired radiograph?
questions.explanation: It lies against the right heart border; consolidation can erase that air-to-soft-tissue interface.

questions.prompt: Does a lobar distribution alone identify a bacterial cause?
questions.explanation: Distribution localizes disease. Lobar consolidation can have other causes, so interpret it with clinical evidence.
